name: Compassion and mercy
question: What does it mean to show mercy, and to whom is it owed?
description: Compassion appears across these traditions as an action, a disposition and sometimes a divine attribute. The passages gathered here do not say the same thing: some ground mercy in God's nature, others in the relief of suffering, others in the recognition of shared vulnerability.

passages.note: The Beatitudes promise mercy to the merciful, linking human practice to divine response.
The opening invocation names God as the Compassionate and Merciful; the formula frames the whole surah.
Mercy is repeated as a divine attribute, not merely an occasional act.
Hatred is ended by love, not by more hatred. The verse is about the cessation of a cycle, not a sentiment.
Goodness and mercy 'follow' the psalmist; the Hebrew חֶסֶד carries covenantal steadfastness as well as tenderness.
Jain non-violence begins with attention to the harm one causes to other living beings.

name: Justice and righteousness
question: What is owed to others, and what makes a society just?
description: Justice is variously imagined as right relation, divine judgement, social fairness and inward integrity. These excerpts show different starting points: covenant, law, virtue, recognition and critique.

passages.note: Hunger and thirst for righteousness: justice as a desire that can be satisfied.
Those persecuted for righteousness are called blessed; the text does not promise that justice is easy or triumphant.
Human diversity is framed as a reason for mutual knowledge; the most honoured are the most God-conscious, not the most powerful.
Harmony is prized, but not at the expense of ritual restraint; social ease requires form.
Socrates treats the examined life as a good worth dying for, raising the question of what a city owes its questioners.

name: Wisdom and knowledge
question: What kind of knowledge changes the person who holds it?
description: Wisdom is rarely mere information in these texts. It is a practised discernment, a way of seeing through appearances, or a form of attention to the real.

passages.note: Learning is pleasant when practised and shared; the passage joins study, friendship and equanimity.
The Way that can be spoken is not the enduring Way; language both discloses and limits.
Mind precedes action; wisdom begins with the quality of intention.
Philosophy is a daily practice of attention to one's own soul and mortality.
Right action is performed for its own sake, not for its fruits; equanimity is called yoga.

name: Death and mortality
question: How should the awareness of death shape a life?
description: Mortality is confronted as enemy, teacher, transition and natural process. The selections are deliberately not harmonised: they disagree about what death means and what consolation is available.

passages.note: The valley of the shadow of death is walked through, not avoided; the psalmist speaks of accompaniment.
Life is a point, a stream and a pilgrimage; philosophy is what can be carried through it.
Socrates refuses to trade the examined life for survival, while admitting uncertainty about death.
God is the Living and Eternal, unlike all that is contingent; the verse is a meditation on dependence.

name: Love and devotion
question: Is love a feeling, a command, a practice or a bond?
description: These passages place love in ethics, worship and kinship. They do not share one concept of love; the notes identify the different vocabularies at work.

passages.note: The Pali term is often rendered loving-kindness (mettā); it is an active practice, not mere warmth.
Mercy is shown in practice and is promised in return.
Covenantal mercy accompanies the speaker through life.
Filial piety and fraternal respect are presented as the root of humaneness (ren).

name: Desire and self-discipline
question: How should a person train desire?
description: Discipline appears as ascetic practice, philosophical attention, ritual cultivation and detachment. The comparison highlights different diagnoses of why desire is dangerous.

passages.note: A chain runs from dwelling on sense objects to desire, passion, recklessness and the ruin of judgement.
Daily self-examination is a practice of fidelity, sincerity and learning.
The Jain path begins with comprehending and renouncing the causes of harm.
The Stoic works on his own judgements and desires as a daily discipline.
The mind is the hinge of ethical action; disciplined intention shapes what follows.

name: The divine and ultimate reality
question: What is ultimately real, and how can it be named?
description: These texts speak of God, the Dao, the Logos and the Eternal. Similar grammar does not establish that they mean the same thing. The notes keep the theological differences visible.

passages.note: God creates the heavens and the earth; the text does not explicitly state creation from nothing.
The Logos is with God and is God; the prologue identifies the Word with the light entering the world.
God is the Living, the Eternal, neither slumbering nor sleeping; sovereignty and knowledge are absolute.
The nameless is the origin of heaven and earth; the named is the mother of the ten thousand things.
The text calls the practitioner to act without attachment, a discipline rooted in a larger account of self and action.

name: Suffering and resilience
question: How do these traditions name suffering, and what do they offer in response?
description: The passages range from diagnosis to lament to practical instruction. They should not be read as interchangeable consolation: some address the nature of mind, others the presence of God, others the fragility of life.

passages.note: Suffering follows corrupt intention as the wheel follows the ox; the claim is causal and ethical.
The world is described as afflicted and full of pain; the response is non-harm and renunciation.
Lament and trust coexist; the speaker does not deny the valley.
The brevity and turbulence of life are met with a disciplined philosophical practice.
Socrates chooses a life of examination even when it leads to danger.

name: Humility and pride
question: What is the difference between humility and self-erasure?
description: Humility is sometimes epistemic (knowing what one does not know), sometimes social (not grasping for status), and sometimes theological (creatureliness before God).

passages.note: Gravity, faithfulness and readiness to correct one's faults are marks of the serious student.
The concern is not being unknown but failing to know others.
Highest excellence is like water: it benefits all things and does not contend.
Status is measured by God-consciousness, not lineage or power.
The meek inherit the earth, a reversal of conventional status.

name: Truthfulness and speech
question: When is speech truthful, and what makes a person trustworthy?
description: Truth is treated as a quality of speech, of intention, of testimony and of reality itself. The notes distinguish these registers rather than collapsing them.

passages.note: Sincere words are not fine; fine words are not sincere. Truth and eloquence are set in tension.
Hold faithfulness and sincerity as first principles.
The quality of intention determines the shape of action and consequence.
The light shines in darkness; truth is figured as illumination that is not overcome.
Socrates insists on speaking the truth even when it costs him his life.

name: Human nature
question: What is a human being, and what can we become?
description: These texts describe humans as created, as capable of virtue, as bundles of habit and intention, and as beings who suffer and learn. The differences are substantive.

passages.note: The Beatitudes begin with the poor in spirit, reversing ordinary measures of worth.
Pure intention produces happiness that follows like a shadow.
Human flourishing is social and practised: learning, friends, equanimity.
The mind can be captured by sense objects; discipline is the art of interrupting the chain.
The capacity to comprehend and renounce the causes of harm is central to Jain anthropology.

name: Community and responsibility
question: What do we owe the communities that form us?
description: Community is imagined as family, covenant, congregation, monastic order and human family. The passages disagree about the boundaries of obligation.

passages.note: Filial piety and fraternal respect are the root of humaneness, grounding ethics in family relations.
Peoples and tribes are made for mutual knowledge, not for supremacy.
Peacemakers are called children of God.
The monk's discipline extends responsibility to all living beings.
The sage gives to others and does not contend; generosity is a way of being in the world.
